name: Communication and Presentation
description:
This course tackles three questions: 
1.	How does a convincing argument look like?
2.	What is the main structure of a convincing argument? 
3.	Why is the way of speaking or writing crucial to build up a convincing argument?                     
Picture this: You go on a Saturday morning to Marienplatz. You want to get fresh air, to have a nice walk and eventually to get a hot chocolate at the Café Glockenspiel. You stop by at this Café and you order an exquisite hot chocolate. You take the menu in your hands and notice that the food is not named. Each dish has a list of all the ingredients and a detailed chart with nutritional information: calories, protein, sugar. 
Ask yourself this: Would you order a dish just by seeing the nutritional facts of it? Or would you rather buy a dish because it has a nice name and the description of the ingredients is full of positive features? If you say yes to the last question, then you are not giving attention to the actual content of the dish but rather you are deciding based on its appearance. 
That is exactly what this laboratory is about: How the appearance of an idea - or a dish - changes its content. We want to sell other people our own ideas. We want to convince them.
Our mean to do so is really simple:  argumentation. On the one side, it is about looking good. So get dressed because we are going to a fancy bal. You are probably not getting in if you wear dirty sneakers, a shirt and training pants. This is called Rhetoric. 
On the other side, it is about being good. So we are not just wearing a nice suit for the bal but also we know that behind that suit there is a good person. A good argument is made of logical relations between sentences. Does it make sense to say that water is not wet? Probably not. That is called Logic. 
Our ideas work exactly like that: How you present them is how people are going to take them. If you want a person to believe in your idea, you need to make it as if you were going to the bal: Your idea needs a nice fancy suit.
Some topics we are going to address are these:
-	Truth theories;
-	Rational Thinking;
-	Deduction and Induction;
-	Types of arguments;
-	Eloquence Vs Rhetoric;
-	Emotional language.
-	Language and Society.
prerequisites: For this course you need to have just one thing: the willingness to learn by experimenting.
